title: Zoom, Don't Wander: Why Regional Search Outperforms Pareto Reasoning and Global Optimization in Budget-Constrained SBSE

edges.target: NSGA-II (Deb et al.)
edges.ref: [9] Deb, Pratap, Agarwal, Meyarivan. A fast and elitist multiobjective genetic algorithm: NSGA-II. IEEE Trans. Evo. Comp., 6(2):182-197, 2002.
edges.evidence: NSGA-II [9] is the one of the most widely cited multi-objective evolutionary algorithm in SBSE [5]... Both are run at 200 (equal-budget comparison) and 1000 evaluations

edges.target: SPEA2 (Zitzler et al.)
edges.ref: [10] Zitzler, Laumanns, Thiele. SPEA2: Improving the strength Pareto evolutionary algorithm. TIK-Report 103, ETH Zurich, 2001.
edges.evidence: SPEA2 [10] provides an archive-based alternative with strength fitness and k-NN density estimation. Including both ensures results are not artifacts of NSGA-II's specific crowding-distance mechanism.

edges.target: SMAC (Hutter et al.)
edges.ref: [11] Hutter, Hoos, Leyton-Brown. Sequential model-based optimization for general algorithm configuration. Proc. LION, pages 507-523. Springer, 2011.
edges.evidence: SMAC [11] fits a Random Forest surrogate over the decision space and uses Expected Improvement to select evaluations, optimising D2H directly.

edges.target: Random-search baseline guideline (Arcuri & Briand)
edges.ref: [25] Arcuri, Briand. A practical guide for using statistical tests to assess randomized algorithms in software engineering. ICSE, pages 1-10. IEEE, 2011.
edges.evidence: Arcuri and Briand [25] demonstrated that random search often provides surprisingly competitive performance in SBSE, making it an essential baseline for any optimization comparison.

edges.target: EZR (Rayegan & Menzies; Menzies & Ganguly)
edges.ref: [13] Rayegan, Menzies. Minimal data, maximum clarity: A heuristic for explaining optimization. arXiv:2509.08667, 2025. [14] Menzies, Ganguly. How low can you go? The data-light SE challenge. Arxiv, 2026.
edges.evidence: We use a minimal contrastive regional search, EZR [13, 14]. It maintains a Best set (sqrt N solutions with lowest D2H found so far) and a Rest set

edges.target: Replication package (ParetoMyth)
edges.ref: https://github.com/kkganguly/ParetoMyth
edges.evidence: Replication package: https://github.com/kkganguly/ParetoMyth.

edges.target: MOOT repository
edges.ref: [4] Menzies, Chen, Ye, Ganguly, Rayegan, Srinivasan, Lustosa. Moot: a repository of many multi-objective optimization tasks. arXiv:2511.16882, 2025.
edges.evidence: We evaluate on MOOT (Multi-Objective Optimization Testing) [4], a repository consolidating over 100 SE optimization tasks drawn from dozens of peer-reviewed publications

edges.target: PromiseTune configuration tasks (Chen & Chen)

edges.evidence: software configuration (e.g., system performance tuning across 25 software systems and 12 PromiseTune tasks [27])

edges.target: Earlier MOOT-using studies as dataset provenance (compact AI, iSNEAK, LLM warm-start, DRR)
edges.ref: [28] Menzies. The case for compact AI. CACM 68(8), 2025; [29] Lustosa, Menzies. iSNEAK. IEEE Access 12, 2024; [30] Senthilkumar, Menzies. arXiv:2501.00125; [31] Lustosa, Menzies. arXiv:2503.21086

edges.target: Scott-Knott recursive bi-clustering (with bootstrap + Cliff's delta)
edges.ref: [47] A. J. Scott and M. Knott. A cluster analysis method for grouping means in the analysis of variance. Biometrics, 30:507-512, 1974.
edges.evidence: We perform statistical comparisons via Scott-Knott recursive bi-clustering method [47]. It clusters optimizers per dataset by recursively splitting ranked distributions only where bootstrap significance and Cliff's Delta effect size both confirm

edges.target: Pairwise Win/Tie/Loss comparison practice (Demsar)
edges.ref: [48] Janez Demsar. Statistical comparisons of classifiers over multiple data sets. JMLR, 7(Jan):1-30, 2006.
edges.evidence: Win/Tie/Loss counts follow the pairwise practice recommended by Demsar [48]: the cheaper method is the reference

edges.target: Equal-weight aggregation / closest-to-ideal selection (Hwang & Yoon; Zeleny) -> D2H metric
edges.ref: [19] Hwang, Yoon. Multiple attribute decision making. Springer, 2012. [20] Zeleny. Multiple Criteria Decision Making. McGraw-Hill, 1982.
edges.evidence: equal-weight aggregation is the theoretically grounded default, and the recommended first point to inspect is the solution closest to the ideal [19, 20]... We therefore use Distance-to-Heaven (D2H)

edges.target: IGD/HV Pareto evaluation guidance (Li, Chen & Yao)
edges.ref: [21] Miqing Li, Tao Chen, Xin Yao. How to evaluate solutions in pareto-based search-based software engineering? A critical review and methodological guidance. IEEE TSE, 2020.
edges.evidence: Li et al. [21] provide standard evaluation guidance using IGD and HV, which our RQ3 follows.

edges.target: Best-vs-Rest decision-tree explanation (Rayegan & Menzies)
edges.ref: [13] Amirali Rayegan and Tim Menzies. Minimal data, maximum clarity: A heuristic for explaining optimization. arXiv:2509.08667, 2025.
edges.evidence: The decision-tree explainability step builds on Rayegan and Menzies [13], which show that shallow Best-vs.-Rest trees produce actionable configuration guidance

edges.target: Prior MOOT benchmark result: SMAC beats TPE/DEHB (Menzies & Ganguly)
edges.ref: [14] Tim Menzies and Kishan Kumar Ganguly. How low can you go? The data-light SE challenge. Arxiv, 2026.
edges.evidence: A prior study on the same MOOT benchmark [14] found it competitive with or better than TPE [23] and DEHB [24], making it a reasonable choice among global Bayesian methods

edges.target: NSGA-II population-size evidence (Hort & Sarro)
edges.ref: [49] Max Hort and Federica Sarro. The effect of offspring population size on NSGA-II: A preliminary study. GECCO, pages 1-2. ACM, 2021.
edges.evidence: population sizes of 10 and 20 for 200 and 1000 evaluation budgets were used respectively, following evidence that smaller populations with more generations improve performance [49]

edges.target: Evaluation-cost measurement from FLASH (Nair et al.)
edges.ref: [16] Vivek Nair, Zhe Yu, Tim Menzies, Norbert Siegmund, Sven Apel. Finding faster configurations using FLASH. IEEE TSE, 46(7):794-811, 2020.
edges.evidence: compiler flag selection requires 35-135 minutes per evaluation [16], and Nair et al. explicitly note that exploring more than a handful of configurations is usually infeasible

edges.target: Expert-elicitation label rate (Valerdi; Easterby-Smith)
edges.ref: [17] Valerdi. Heuristics for systems engineering cost estimation. IEEE Sys. J., 2010. [18] Easterby-Smith. The design, analysis and interpretation of repertory grids. IJMMS 13(1), 1980.
edges.evidence: similarly, expert elicitation yields roughly ten labels per session [17, 18]. In such settings ... cap realistic budgets well below 1,000 evaluations

edges.target: Pareto-vs-weighted SBSE study (Chen & Li) - baseline selection and population assumptions
edges.ref: [7] J. Chen and M. Li. The weights can be harmful: Pareto search versus weighted search in multi-objective SBSE. ACM TOSEM, 32:1-40, 2023.
edges.evidence: NSGA-II and SPEA2 were selected as the most widely used Pareto methods in SBSE [7], reflecting standard community practice.

edges.target: SSBSE usage survey ranking (Colanzi et al.)
edges.ref: [22] Colanzi, Assuncao, Vergilio, Farah, Guizzo, et al. The symposium on search-based software engineering: Past, present and future. IST 127:106372, 2020.
edges.evidence: As per Colanzi et al., it is the second most widely used optimizers in SBSE over the past decade [22].

edges.target: Multi-objective theory: Pareto fronts may span the whole objective space (Hwang & Yoon; Zeleny)
edges.ref: [19] Hwang, Yoon. Multiple attribute decision making. Springer, 2012. [20] Zeleny. Multiple Criteria Decision Making. McGraw-Hill, 1982.
edges.evidence: They occupy a tight cluster in decision space while simultaneously sitting in the near-ideal region of objective space, rather than being dispersed across it as multi-objective theory permits [19, 20].
edges.section: 2.3 Zoom Search Trajectories Cover the Pareto Front

edges.target: Prior result: Pareto search wins given sufficient budget (Chen & Li)
edges.ref: [7] J. Chen and M. Li. The weights can be harmful: Pareto search versus weighted search in multi-objective SBSE. ACM TOSEM, 32:1-40, 2023.
edges.evidence: Chen and Li [7] showed Pareto search wins given sufficient convergence budget. We complement this by analysing where and why Pareto methods fail across 100+ SE datasets under sub-convergence budgets

edges.target: SBSE survey: NSGA-II most widely cited MOEA (Harman et al.)
edges.ref: [5] Mark Harman, S Afshin Mansouri, Yuanyuan Zhang. Search-based software engineering: Trends, techniques and applications. ACM CSUR, 45(1):11, 2012.
edges.evidence: NSGA-II [9] is the one of the most widely cited multi-objective evolutionary algorithm in SBSE [5].

edges.target: Few master variables govern SE solution quality (PromiseTune; Chen & Chen)
edges.ref: [27] Pengzhou Chen, Tao Chen. Promisetune: Unveiling causally promising and explainable configuration tuning. ICSE 2026.
edges.evidence: PromiseTune [27] suggests why: few master variables govern SE solution quality.
edges.section: 8 Related Work; 6.2 (identifies the few master variables and bounds [14, 27])

edges.target: Prior finding: SE problems collapse into few occupied regions (Menzies & Ganguly)
edges.ref: [14] Tim Menzies and Kishan Kumar Ganguly. How low can you go? The data-light SE challenge. Arxiv, 2026.
edges.evidence: Menzies and Ganguly [14] further show that SE problems collapse into surprisingly few occupied regions.
edges.section: 8 Related Work; 2.1 (bottleneck is candidate evaluation cost [14, 16])

notes: No replication edges: the landscape analysis is new and no prior experiment is re-run; five v1 sanitychecks became numericfact, one became methodology; new edges capture the refutes-polarity uses of [19,20] (MO theory) and [7] (Pareto wins with budget); self=true only for refs sharing Menzies/Ganguly.
